## {{< meta title >}}
<!-- MARKDOWN COMMENT: Replace the instructions below with your a brief overview or abstract of your presentation -->

Hello there! 👋 I'm Matt Christie, a data engineer at University of Wisconsin-Madison's
[Global Land Use and Environment Lab](https://www.gibbs-lab.wisc.edu/) (GLUE). It was a
privilege and a pleasure to present on Git today, an invaluable and omnipresent tool for
version control. I wanted to give as close to a comprehensive overview as I could in 90
minutes, starting from simple objects like files and folders and building up to how we use
Git to manage our real-world projects.

While many sources cite code backups and collaboration as primary reasons to use the tool,
one of the main things I find myself using it for is communication. With judicious use of
commits, branches, and pull requests, I like that Git allows me to advertise and explain
my project in bite-sized pieces that map clearly onto what I'd like others (and myself) to
know about it. In an attempt to highlight this aspect of its use, I presented the tutorial
as [The Story of Your Project](https://youtu.be/7x6C8_FXEK0?si=Kb8MASIoMIJCwup0) (posted on YouTube).
Looking back, the tutorial ended up being more focused on the specific operations Git makes
possible, though it's my hope that at least some of this appreciation still shines through.

I've also used AI to generate [companion tutorial materials](https://github.com/glue-lab/uw-rse-git-tutorial)
from the video content that are hosted on my lab's GitHub. The repository contains
markdown files that largely follow the content of the video and provide concise explanations
of the commands it covers. I've reviewed the materials manually and have made small updates
for clarity and correctness.

Enjoy! 📖
